pages.title: Features
pages.content:
Features

One workspace for the whole product cycle

From the first idea to the release note, Orbitly keeps context in one place so nobody has to ask where things stand.

Plan

Boards that keep up with you

Move cards with the keyboard, set work-in-progress limits per column and split a sprint without losing history.

  • Keyboard-first: J, K and arrow keys everywhere
  • Swimlanes by owner, priority or label
  • Sprint scope changes recorded automatically

Measure

Reports without the spreadsheet

Cycle time, throughput and goal progress update live. Every Friday, a plain-language summary lands in your inbox.

  • Twelve built-in charts and a custom chart builder
  • Share a read-only link with stakeholders
  • Export to CSV or straight to your data warehouse

Connect

Plays well with your stack

Link commits to tasks, post updates to chat and sync due dates with your calendar. Two-way, real time, no glue code.

Browse integrations

See it with your own data

Import from your current tool in one click and keep your history.

Questions, answered

Can I change plans later?

Yes. Upgrades apply immediately and are prorated; downgrades take effect at the end of the billing period.

What counts as an active member?

Anyone who signs in or is mentioned in a comment during the billing month. Guests and viewers are always free.

Do you offer discounts for non-profits and schools?

We offer 50% off the Team plan for registered non-profits and accredited schools. Write to us from the contact page.

Where is my data stored?

In the EU or the US, your choice, encrypted at rest and in transit. Enterprise plans can pin data to a single region.

pages.title: About Orbitly
pages.excerpt: A remote team of sixty-two building a calmer way to plan.
pages.content:
Orbitly started in 2021 as a side project between three people who were tired of spending Monday mornings asking where things stood. Today we are a remote team of sixty-two across eleven time zones, and we still plan every week in our own product.

What we believe

  • Calm beats busy. Software should reduce noise, not add to it.
  • Defaults matter. Most teams never change settings, so ours should be good ones.
  • Ship small, ship often. We release something every week and write about it in the changelog.

By the numbers

teams using Orbitly

We build the tool we want to use on a Monday morning: quiet, quick and honest about where things stand.

posts.title: Orbitly 2.0: a calmer workspace, rebuilt from the ground up
posts.excerpt: A new navigation, a three-times faster editor, dark mode and a home screen that shows only what changed since you last looked.
posts.content:
Two years ago we shipped the first version of Orbitly to forty teams. Today more than a hundred thousand plan their week with it, and the product had grown in every direction at once. Version 2.0 is the result of six months spent putting it back in order.

  • Released: 21 October 2026
  • Plans: all
  • Migration: automatic

What changed

  • NewA home screen that shows only what changed since your last visit.
  • NewDark mode that follows your system, with a high-contrast option.
  • ImprovedThe editor is three times faster on large documents.
  • ImprovedNavigation fits on one line: Home, Work, Reports, Settings.
  • FixedComments no longer jump when someone edits above them.

Why we rebuilt instead of patching

Every feature we added made the next one harder. The sidebar had nineteen entries; settings lived in four places. We wrote down the ten things people do most and designed around those, then found homes for everything else.

The best compliment we heard in the beta was that it felt like the app had gone quiet.

Product design team

Your workspace moves to 2.0 automatically over the next week. Nothing is deleted, and you can switch back from Settings until the end of the year if you need more time.

posts.title: Automations get branches, delays and a visual editor
posts.excerpt: Draw a process as a flow, branch on any field, wait for approvals and see a preview of every path before you switch it on.
posts.content:
Automations were the most used and the most confusing part of Orbitly. People loved what they did and hated building them in a list of dropdowns. Today the builder becomes a canvas.

Branches and delays

Any step can now split on a condition: plan, priority, a custom field or the person who made the request. Delays wait for a fixed time, a date field or until someone approves.

  • NewVisual flow editor with drag-and-drop steps.
  • NewBranch on any field, with up to five paths per step.
  • NewDelay until a time, a date field or an approval.
  • ImprovedEvery automation shows its last fifty runs with inputs and outputs.

Test before you trust

Preview mode runs your flow against a real item without changing anything and highlights the path it would take. It is the feature beta testers asked for most, and the one we use the most ourselves.

Automations 2.0 is available on every plan. Starter workspaces keep their limit of ten runs a month.

comments.author: Tomás L.
comments.content: Preview mode saved me from emailing two hundred customers by accident. Great addition.

posts.title: Introducing the public REST API and webhooks
posts.excerpt: Everything you can do in the app, you can now do with a documented REST API, plus signed webhooks for every event.
posts.content:
Our internal API has powered the Orbitly apps since day one. Starting today, the same API is public, versioned and documented, with personal tokens and OAuth apps.

A first request

curl https://api.orbitly.example/v1/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ORBITLY_TOKEN" \
  -d title="Draft the release note" \
  -d project=launch-week

Responses are JSON, lists are paginated with cursors and every write accepts an idempotency key, so retries are safe.

Webhooks

  • Subscribe to forty event types, from task.created to sprint.closed.
  • Every delivery is signed with a secret you can rotate.
  • Failed deliveries retry with backoff for twenty-four hours.

Read the reference, try requests in the browser and generate a token from Settings, then Developer. Rate limits are generous: six hundred requests a minute per workspace.

posts.title: Weekly reports now write their own summary
posts.excerpt: Every Friday, a short plain-language summary of what shipped, what slipped and what is at risk, built from the work itself.
posts.content:
Status reports take time to write and are out of date when they are read. The new weekly summary is assembled from what actually happened in your workspace, so nobody has to write it.

What it includes

  1. What shipped, grouped by project
  2. What slipped and by how much
  3. Items at risk, with the reason in one line
  4. Cycle time compared with the previous four weeks

Private by design

Summaries are generated in your workspace region and never leave it. You can edit one before it is sent, and turn the feature off per project.

Early teams told us the summary changed how their Friday felt: instead of writing about the week, they read about it, added a sentence of context and moved on.

posts.title: Single sign-on and audit logs for every Team plan
posts.excerpt: Security features should not be a reason to buy a bigger plan. SAML single sign-on, SCIM provisioning and audit logs are now part of Team.
posts.content:
Until now, single sign-on was an Enterprise feature. We heard from many small teams that went through a security review and had to explain why the tool they liked did not support it. That changes today.

Now on the Team plan

Audit logs record sign-ins, permission changes, exports and deletions. You can filter them in the app or stream them to your security tooling with a webhook.

Paying more for basic security made us the bad guys in every review. We would rather be the easy yes.

Our security lead

posts.title: Sprint boards: faster drag, keyboard moves and WIP limits
posts.excerpt: Boards with a thousand cards now scroll at sixty frames a second, cards move with the keyboard, and columns can limit work in progress.
posts.content:
Boards are where most teams spend their day, so small frictions add up. This release is a collection of fixes for the ones you reported most.

In this release

  • ImprovedRendering is virtualised: large boards stay smooth.
  • NewMove a card with Shift and the arrow keys.
  • NewWork-in-progress limits per column, with a gentle warning.
  • FixedFilters are kept when you switch between board and list.

The new renderer only draws the cards you can see, which also cut memory use on large boards by two thirds. Older laptops and tablets benefit the most.

Limits that nudge, not block

Work-in-progress limits are off by default. Turn them on from a column’s menu; the column header turns amber when the limit is reached and nothing is ever blocked.

posts.title: 40 new integrations, and how we pick what to build
posts.excerpt: Calendars, design tools, support desks and two dozen more. Here is the list, and the simple rule we use to decide what comes next.
posts.content:
This quarter we shipped forty new integrations, bringing the total past one hundred and twenty. Rather than a long list, here is how we choose.

The rule

We build an integration when at least two hundred workspaces ask for it and we can make it two-way. A one-way sync that copies data and forgets about it creates more questions than it answers.

Most requested

  • Calendar sync
  • Design file previews
  • Support desk tickets

Coming next

  • Accounting exports
  • Video call recaps
  • Status page updates

Vote for the next ones from Settings, then Integrations. Every request is read by the team that builds them.

posts.title: 100,000 teams: what we learned getting here
posts.excerpt: Five lessons from four years of building a planning tool, from the feature we deleted to the support habit we will never drop.
posts.content:
Last week the hundred-thousandth team created a workspace. Milestones are a good excuse to look back, so here are five things we learned on the way.

Five lessons

  1. Delete more. Removing our timeline view made the product better and almost nobody missed it.
  2. Answer every email. Engineers rotate through support every month.
  3. Write it down. The changelog keeps us honest about what we actually shipped.
  4. Price for small teams. They grow into big ones.
  5. Stay boring about infrastructure. Uptime is a feature.

What comes next

The next year is about depth rather than breadth: faster search, better offline support and the reporting features larger teams keep asking for.

Thank you to every team that took a chance on a small product. We are just getting started.
